context: Void reactivity coefficient αv = +4 to +8 pcm per 1% increase in steam void fraction; 1 pcm = 10^-5 Δk/k; at full power (1200-1600 MWe); 2.0% enrichment fuel (pre-1987); positive because graphite is primary moderator (not water); water acts as parasitic absorber
notes: At 100% steam void (catastrophic loss of coolant): +4 to +8% Δk/k = +0.8 to +1.6 β_eff (β_eff≈0.005); positive feedback possible but normally offset by Doppler at high power; the void coefficient is the fundamental instability that made Chernobyl Unit 4 dangerous at low power
source: INSAG-7 Section 4; OECD-NEA Ch.I; reactor_physics_REAL.csv; Boure 1997 Prog Nucl Energy

context: Below 700 MWt thermal: void coefficient increases in magnitude; αv = +6 to +10 pcm/%void; at these conditions, loss of 1% coolant void adds 0.006-0.010% Δk/k; Doppler feedback (temperature coefficient) is small at low temperature → net power coefficient becomes POSITIVE = unstable
notes: The forbidden operating zone below 700 MWt was defined because reactor becomes power-unstable: positive power coefficient means a brief power surge heats coolant → more steam → more positive reactivity → accelerating power surge; RBMK procedure prohibited operation <700 MWt; Chernobyl Unit 4 was at ~200 MWt during test

context: Pressurized Water Reactor: void coefficient strongly NEGATIVE; water is BOTH moderator AND coolant; when water leaves channel: BOTH moderation AND absorption decrease, but moderation loss dominates → fewer neutrons thermalized → reduced fission → negative feedback; fundamental thermodynamic stability of Western PWR design
notes: The RBMK vs PWR void coefficient sign reversal is the fundamental physics difference that made RBMK uniquely dangerous; in a PWR, any loss-of-coolant accident self-limits because void removes moderator; in RBMK, void ADDS reactivity because graphite provides moderation regardless
source: Glasstone Sesonske Nuclear Reactor Engineering; Lamarsh; reactor_physics_REAL.csv

context: Graphite moderator temperature coefficient: negative (as graphite heats, phonon vibrations increase, neutron spectrum hardens slightly, reduced thermal fission probability); magnitude small: -1 to -2 pcm/°C; provides some stabilizing feedback from graphite heating
notes: Graphite Tm coefficient is stabilizing but small; graphite temperature changes slowly (large thermal mass); provides delayed negative feedback; contrasted with fast positive void coefficient from steam generation; net effect: void feedback wins over graphite feedback on accident timescales

context: Fuel Doppler coefficient (nuclear resonance broadening): as fuel temperature increases, U-238 absorption resonances broaden (Doppler broadening) → more U-238 neutron capture → fewer neutrons available → negative reactivity feedback; magnitude -2 to -4 pcm/°C fuel temperature; instantaneous feedback (temperature tracks power on millisecond timescale)
notes: Doppler coefficient is the primary safety mechanism in all uranium-bearing reactors; it is negative and instantaneous; in RBMK at high power: Doppler provides -2 to -4 pcm/°C; with fuel temperature change of several hundred °C during power surge → hundreds of pcm negative feedback; BUT at low power (200 MWt), fuel temperature is low, temperature changes are small, Doppler feedback is small

context: At >700 MWt: net power coefficient (sum of void + Doppler + other thermal feedbacks) is negative = stable; power disturbances self-correct; if power rises → temperature rises → Doppler adds negative reactivity → power returns to set point; this is why RBMK operated safely at high power for years
notes: RBMK units operated thousands of reactor-years at high power without accidents after proper modification; the design was safe at high power; the accident required low power (xenon poisoning forced low power) combined with nearly all rods withdrawn (ORM=8)
source: INSAG-7; WNA RBMK reactor overview; OECD-NEA

context: Below 700 MWt: void coefficient (positive) > Doppler + graphite (negative) → net positive power coefficient = unstable regime; any power perturbation amplifies; this is the forbidden operating zone where Chernobyl Unit 4 was operating during the test on April 26 1986
notes: This positive power coefficient at low power was: (a) known to Soviet reactor physicists; (b) documented in RBMK technical specifications; (c) addressed by procedural prohibition on <700 MWt operation; (d) ignored by operators on April 26; this knowledge being withheld from operators was part of the safety culture failure

context: Why RBMK void coefficient is positive: (1) graphite (C-12) is primary moderator (moderating ratio ~170 for graphite vs ~59 for H2O); (2) graphite fills ALL space between fuel channels; (3) water fills ONLY the ~8cm pressure tubes; (4) water acts primarily as parasitic absorber (NOT primary moderator); (5) when water boils/is removed → absorption decreases → k_eff increases
notes: Compare CANDU (also graphite moderator + water coolant): CANDU void coefficient also slightly positive; both designs have this physics; difference: CANDU has on-line refueling and different geometry that limits the void coefficient magnitude; both differ fundamentally from LWR where water is primary moderator
source: INSAG-7; OECD-NEA; Cottingham 2011 Energy Environ Sci; Lamarsh

context: When AZ-5 SCRAM pressed: control rods INSERT into core; rod design has graphite displacer tips; bottom 1.5m of each rod = graphite (displaces water from that zone when rod enters from bottom); as rod enters bottom of channel, graphite DISPLACES water → water absorption removed → positive reactivity for first 2-3 seconds
notes: This is the proximate physical cause of the Chernobyl excursion: pressing AZ-5 SCRAM at 01:23:40 with ORM=8 and reactor at 200 MWt caused +2-3β positive reactivity spike BEFORE rods could add negative reactivity; combined with existing positive void feedback from steam generation → prompt criticality

context: At moment of AZ-5 press: (a) reactivity already near threshold due to coolant boiling (void) + ORM=8 (nearly all rods withdrawn); (b) graphite tip effect added +2-3β; (c) steam void increase as power started to rise added further positive reactivity; (d) total positive reactivity estimated +7-10β >> prompt criticality threshold (+1β)
notes: This level of positive reactivity (+7-10β) means reactor was +6-9β superprompt-critical; power excursion timescale = microseconds to milliseconds; uncontrollable mechanically; no human intervention possible; steam explosion within 3-4 seconds; reactor destroyed
source: INSAG-7 Table 4.1; reactor_physics_REAL.csv; prompt criticality definition: ρ > β_eff

context: After 1987-1989 modifications: void coefficient reduced from +4-8 pcm/%void to +0.5-2 pcm/%void; achieved by: (1) fuel enrichment 2.0→2.8% (changes neutron balance); (2) additional absorbers in core (fixed absorbers); (3) modified rod design eliminating graphite tip positive spike; (4) minimum ORM raised from 15 to 30 rods
notes: Modified RBMK is safer: at 100% void: +0.5-2% Δk/k = +0.1-0.4β = below prompt criticality threshold even without other feedback; still positive void coefficient (unlike LWR) but magnitude too small to cause prompt criticality alone; 11 RBMK still operating Russia 2026 with these modifications

context: Delayed neutron fraction β_eff: U-235 thermal fission = 0.0065 (0.65%); Pu-239 thermal fission = 0.0021 (0.21%); Unit 4 core at accident had mixed fuel (fresh U-235 channels + aged channels with some Pu-239 buildup); effective β_eff ≈ 0.005; lower β_eff means prompt criticality achieved at LOWER excess reactivity
notes: Pu-239's lower β_eff means Pu-fueled reactors have less margin against prompt criticality; in Unit 4 at accident time: mixed fuel means β_eff ≈ 0.005; this is the β used in ρ>β prompt criticality definition
source: NNDC delayed neutron data; Keepin GR 1965 Physics of Nuclear Kinetics; xenon_135_poisoning_REAL.csv

context: Control rod full insertion time (AZ-5 SCRAM) = 18-20 seconds from signal to full insertion; compare: Western PWR SCRAM time < 2 seconds (gravity-driven rods from top); RBMK rods enter from BOTTOM (motor-driven); 18-20 second delay = reactor physics control impossible during rapid excursion
notes: 18-20 second SCRAM time meant: even if no graphite tip effect, a power surge developing on 1-second timescale cannot be controlled mechanically; this fundamental design flaw was modified post-accident to 12 seconds but still far slower than Western PWR
source: INSAG-7 Section 4.2; rbmk_safety_modifications_REAL.csv; 12-second post-1987 SCRAM time

context: Prompt criticality: reactor is critical on prompt neutrons ALONE (without delayed neutrons); occurs when reactivity ρ > β_eff; below this (1 < k_eff < 1+β) reactor is delayed-supercritical: power rises on delayed neutron timescale (seconds to minutes) = controllable; above prompt criticality: power rises on PROMPT timescale (microseconds to milliseconds) = UNCONTROLLABLE
notes: At Chernobyl: estimated ρ reached +7-10 β_eff = 7-10x above prompt criticality; power increase timescale was ~1-10 milliseconds; no mechanical or electronic system can respond in milliseconds; inevitable catastrophic failure once ρ > β_eff
